newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Still hope for renewed IRA truce - Morrison.
newsitem.headline: Still hope for renewed IRA truce - Morrison.

text.p: A former U.S. congressman leading a fact-finding tour of Northern Ireland said on Tuesday that there was still hope of a renewed ceasefire despite the seizure of IRA arms and explosives in Britain.
Bruce Morrison told reporters after a meeting with Irish Prime Minister John Bruton that a new Irish Republican Army truce was essential for a lasting peace in Northern Ireland.
"There is not a blank wall, there is a small door and it's difficult to open but it's there," he said.

Morrison, who helped broker the original IRA ceasefire, reaffirmed U.S. President Bill Clinton's commitment to peace in the British-ruled province but added that the stalled peace talks must make some progress.
"We need affirmation all round that we don't have an infinite number of choices. There is a process in place, with all its imperfections, that has to be made to work."

Morrison said he believed that Sinn Fein, the political arm of the IRA, wanted a renewal of the 17-month ceasefire that was shattered with a bomb in London's Docklands financial district in February which killed two people and injured more than 100.
Hopes of any chance of a new ceasefire seemed to have been dashed on Monday when British police seized 10 tonnes of explosives after dawn raids in London.
One man was killed in the raids and five others were being questioned by police in London. One of men is a British Airways engineer working at Britain's Gatwick airport.
Police also searched several homes near the border with British-ruled Northern Ireland early on Tuesday but no arrests were made.

Police said they believed the IRA were within hours of launching lorry bomb attacks and targeting public figures. The media speculated that IRA targets ranged from the royal family to the Channel Tunnel between France and Britain.
The IRA has accused London of reneging on a deal to give Sinn Fein a seat in the peace talks by introducing a demand for it to surrender its weapons.
Wrangling over "arms decommissioning" has blighted multi-party talks that started in June. Britain and Ireland have barred Sinn Fein while the IRA remains on a war footing.

Morrison had talks with Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams on Saturday. His five-day intinerary included meetings with most key pro-British and pro-Irish parties. He will brief White House officials and other American politicians when he returns to Washington.
